newsitem.title: GERMANY: SPD says Russian can't copy German deal for NATO.
newsitem.headline: SPD says Russian can't copy German deal for NATO.

text.p: Germany's opposition Social Democrats said on Thursday Russia could not expect the same kind of security guarantees for Eastern European NATO members that it got from Bonn for former East German territory.

Guenter Verheugen, the party's leading foreign policy expert, noted that Bonn conceded to Moscow in 1990 a ban on foreign troops or atomic weapons similar to that which Russia is demanding for any East European states entering NATO.
But he said the eastern states seeking NATO membership would not accept such a limitation to their sovereignty and the Atlantic Alliance could not sign such a document in their name.
"I don't think this can be settled in a treaty-like document," Verheugen told German radio.
"We have to tell the Russians very clearly that that would be a classic case of a treaty to the detriment of a third party, which I think is not possible."
Bonn agreed to limits on troops in eastern Germany as part of the complex negotiations that led to the Two Plus Four treaty in September 1990 and German unification a month later.

In the Two Plus Four treaty, hammered out by the two Germanys with World War Two victors the United States, Soviet Union, Britain and France, Bonn agreed only to allow German troops onto the territory of former East Germany.
"It is even agreed in the treaty that no atomic weapons and no foreign troops can be stationed there," he added.

"Of course, the states that want to become members (of NATO) clearly reject such a settlement in a treaty with Russia, because they say this concerns their sovereignty and their territory. NATO has made clear it does not even intend to move troops there in peacetime or station atomic weapons there."

Russia has recently upped the ante on the security issue, trying to rule out any improvement of military installations and limit upgrades in communications facilities of prospective new members such as Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
NATO, set to issue formal membership invitations in July, says it cannot allow the creation of a second-class membership.
